overview.bigIdea: Mathematics is the **search for patterns – and for the reasons why they happen**. In this chapter you learn the famous number sequences, draw them as dot pictures, and use the pictures to explain surprising links between them.

ladder.a: Name the sequence and find the next terms

overview.languagesTitle: Three ways to show a pattern

languages.name: Pictures
languages.text: Dots arranged in a triangle show *why* the rule works.

plan.text: Lesson 1. Say each rule aloud and write the next three terms.
Lesson 2. Draw triangular, square and hexagonal dot pictures yourself.
Lessons 3–4. Learn the relations with their pictures – these are 2- and 3-mark questions.
Check knowledge quiz, then the revision sheet after 1, 3 and 7 days.

lessons.title: Number sequences
lessons.hook: Your class roll numbers, the days on a calendar, the steps of a staircase – all follow a rule. A **number sequence** is a list of numbers that follows a rule, and spotting that rule is the first skill of a mathematician.

core.def: The branch of mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers.
Numbers written in order following a rule, e.g. 2, 4, 6, 8, …
1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … each is the **sum of the two before it**.

explain: To find the rule, look at the **gaps** between terms. Constant gap → add the same number (odd, even). Growing gaps → triangular, square. Multiplying → powers.
Virahānka numbers are named after the Indian scholar Virahānka, who found them while studying rhythms in poetry – long before they became famous in Europe.

steps: (b) Each term = sum of the two before: 5 + 8 = 13, 8 + 13 = 21, 13 + 21 = 34.

mistakes: Adding a fixed number to Virahānka numbers instead of adding the previous two.
Forgetting that the powers of 2 start at 1 (2⁰ = 1).
lessons.tip: When asked ‘write the rule’, write it in words AND show one example (e.g. ‘add the two previous numbers: 5 + 8 = 13’).
lessons.memory: Gaps constant → add. Gaps growing → triangular/squares. Terms multiplying → powers.
examAsk: Name the sequence and write the next 3 terms.
Which number is both a square and a cube? (64)
Write the rule of a sequence in your own words.

lessons.title: Visualising number sequences
lessons.hook: Why are 1, 4, 9, 16 called **square** numbers? Because that many dots make a perfect square! Drawing a sequence turns a list of numbers into a picture you can *see* and *explain*.

core.def: Dots arranged in a triangle: rows of 1, 2, 3, … dots.
Dots arranged in an n × n square.
Small cubes stacked into a bigger n × n × n cube.
1, 7, 19, 37, 61, … – dots in a hexagon around a centre dot. Gaps: 6, 12, 18, 24 …

explain: The 5th triangular number is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15. A quick way: n × (n + 1) ÷ 2, so the 10th is 10 × 11 ÷ 2 = 55.
Hexagonal numbers grow by adding a ring of 6, 12, 18, … dots around the previous hexagon.

example.q: The dot pictures show 1, 7, 19, 37. Name the sequence and find the next number.
steps: They are arranged as hexagons, so these are **hexagonal numbers**.
example.answer: Hexagonal numbers; next is 61. (Model paper Q27b asks to name 1, 7, 19, 37.)

mistakes: Counting the dots in only the outer ring.
Drawing uneven rows so the picture no longer shows the pattern.
lessons.tip: In a picture question, label each shape with its number of dots underneath – the examiner can see your count.
lessons.memory: Triangle rows 1, 2, 3 … · Square n × n · Hexagon rings of 6, 12, 18 …
examAsk: Draw the next picture in the sequence.
Name the sequence shown by the dots (triangular / square / hexagonal).
How many dots in the 6th square picture?

diagram.caption: Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10 – each new row adds one more dot.

play.title: Dot builder
play.say: Slide to grow the shape. The orange dots show what each new step adds.

lessons.title: Relations among number sequences
lessons.hook: Add odd numbers: 1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. **Square numbers appear!** Mathematicians don't stop at the surprise – they ask *why*, and a picture answers it.

core.def: 1 + 3 + 5 + … (first n odd numbers) = n × n (a square).
1, 1+2, 1+2+3, … gives the **triangular numbers**.
1+3, 3+6, 6+10, … give the square numbers 4, 9, 16 …
(1, 1+2, 1+2+4, …) + 1 = powers of 2 · 6 × triangular + 1 = hexagonal · adding hexagonal numbers gives cubes.

explain: **The picture proof:** split a square of dots into L-shapes. The L-shapes have 1, 3, 5, 7, … dots. So adding odd numbers must give a square – for any size of square.
Using this, the sum of the first 10 odd numbers is 10 × 10 = 100, and the first 100 odd numbers add to 100 × 100 = 10,000 – no long addition needed.

example.q: Show that adding counting numbers gives triangular numbers. (Model paper Q22, 2 marks)
steps: Picture: rows of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 dots stacked make triangles.
example.answer: Adding counting numbers gives the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …

mistakes: Counting how many odd numbers wrongly: 1 + 3 + … + 19 has 10 terms, not 19.
Stopping at the pattern without the picture/explanation when the question says ‘explain’.
lessons.tip: For ‘explain why’ questions, draw the dot picture (L-shapes in a square or rows in a triangle). A clear picture can earn the full marks.
lessons.memory: Odd numbers add to SQUARES. Counting numbers add to TRIANGLES.
examAsk: Sum of the first 10 (or 100) odd numbers.
What do you get when you add consecutive triangular numbers? Explain with a picture.

diagram.caption: Each coloured L-shape adds the next odd number (1, 3, 5, 7) – together they make a square.

play.title: Odd numbers build squares
play.say: Add the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 … one at a time as L-shapes and watch a square appear.

lessons.title: Patterns in shapes
lessons.hook: Shapes have patterns too – and hidden inside them are the same number sequences! Count the little squares in a growing square and you get 1, 4, 9, 16 … the square numbers again. **Geometry** is the study of patterns in shapes.

core.def: Equal sides and equal angles. Sides: 3, 4, 5, 6, … (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon …). Corners = sides.
Every point joined to every other point. Lines: K2 = 1, K3 = 3, K4 = 6, K5 = 10 → **triangular numbers**.
Little squares: 1, 4, 9, 16 → **square numbers**.
Little triangles: 1, 4, 9, 16 (rows 1, 3, 5, 7) → **square numbers**.
Each segment becomes 4: 3, 12, 48, 192, … (3 × powers of 4).

explain: To link a shape to a sequence, **count one thing** in each shape (sides, lines, little squares) and write the numbers in order. Then match the list to Table 1.
For stacked triangles, count row by row: 1, 3, 5, 7 – you are adding odd numbers, which you already know gives squares.

example.q: The number of squares in the Stacked Squares sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, … (a) Find the number in the 5th shape. (b) Which sequence is this? (Model paper Q26, 2 marks)
steps: The nth shape is an n × n square.

mistakes: Counting only the outline squares instead of all little squares.
Saying complete graph lines are square numbers (they are triangular).
Thinking a regular polygon means ‘any polygon with 4 sides’.
lessons.tip: Case-study questions (4 marks) often give a garden, tiles or chairs in a pattern. First write the numbers as a list, name the sequence, then answer each part.
lessons.memory: Polygons → counting numbers from 3 · Complete graphs → triangular · Stacked squares/triangles → squares.
examAsk: How many little squares in the nth shape of Stacked Squares?
Count lines in complete graphs; which sequence?
Case study: flowers/tiles arranged in square patterns.

cards.q: Little triangles in the 3rd stacked triangle?

play.title: Join every dot
play.say: Add points and join each one to every other point. Count the lines – do you know this sequence?

revision: Mathematics is the search for patterns and the reasons why they happen.
Number theory = patterns in whole numbers; geometry = patterns in shapes.
Learn Table 1: all 1’s, counting, odd, even, triangular, squares, cubes, Virahānka, powers of 2 and 3.
Virahānka: each number is the sum of the previous two (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34).
Adding odd numbers from 1 gives squares; adding counting numbers gives triangular numbers.
Up-and-down sums give squares; consecutive triangular numbers add to squares.
(1 + 2 + 4 + …) + 1 gives powers of 2; 6 × triangular + 1 gives hexagonal; adding hexagonal numbers gives cubes.
Regular polygon: equal sides and equal angles; sides 3, 4, 5, … Complete graph lines are triangular numbers.
Stacked squares and stacked triangles both give square numbers; Koch snowflake 3, 12, 48, 192.

paper.what: Adding counting numbers gives triangular numbers – with a picture
Stacked squares: count squares and name the sequence
Case study: flowers in a square number pattern

sections.title: Sequence questions · 3 steps
items: Write the gaps between terms under the sequence.
Name the sequence (triangular, square, Virahānka …) and state its rule in words.
Use the rule to find the missing or next terms – show one line of working for each.

sections.title: Picture questions
items: Draw neat dots or squares in rows; do not squeeze them.
Write the number of dots under each picture.
For ‘explain why’, colour or outline the L-shapes / rows that make the pattern.

sections.title: Answer writing
items: Write the rule or definition in one line first, then apply it – rule lines earn marks even if the arithmetic slips.
Show every step on its own line (for example each division in a prime factorisation or each Kaprekar round).
Underline or box the final answer and write the unit (°, students, books) where there is one.
For ‘Give reason / Justify’ questions: state the rule, then show that the number or figure fits (or does not fit) it.

checklist: I can name all ten sequences in Table 1 and continue each.
I can draw triangular, square and hexagonal dot pictures.
I can find the nth triangular or square number.
I can explain with a picture why adding odd numbers gives squares.
I know which sequence complete graphs, stacked squares and stacked triangles give.
I can solve a pattern case study step by step.

method: Built on proven learning methods: see it as a picture first, understand why it works, learn from worked examples, then test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
